passage:
Zainab, you asked why I turned down that scholarship from the trader. Sit, I'll tell you. I'm Gurpreet. In my second year, Ramlal-ji, a cloth trader from our town, paid my hostel fees. He said it was nothing. But every Sunday afterwards he rang: "Who are your friends? Why was your mark low in physics?" Once he said, "After all I've spent, you should be in the library, not at that match." I began to hide my phone. I felt watched, and I felt I owed him my whole life.
Around then, my old teacher, Mrs Iyer, quietly paid my exam form fee, handed me the receipt and said, "Don't mention it, it's done." I remember standing straighter.
I repaid Ramlal-ji in small parts over three years, and thanked him each time. It was the first time in my life I felt free of him.

qa.q: Who paid Gurpreet's hostel fees in the second year?
qa.a: Ramlal-ji, a cloth trader from Gurpreet's town, paid the hostel fees.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling after the Sunday phone calls began?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt uneasy, watched and deeply indebted, hiding the phone and feeling that a whole life was owed to Ramlal-ji. The questions about friends and marks felt like ownership, not help.

qa.q: What choice did Gurpreet make that eventually gave a sense of freedom?
qa.a: Gurpreet repaid Ramlal-ji in small parts over three years and thanked him each time. That let the help become something finished, not a hold on Gurpreet's life.

qa.q: How might Ramlal-ji have seen his Sunday calls?
qa.a: Probably as caring interest, and perhaps as his right after paying the fees. For Gurpreet they felt like being watched, which shows how help can mean different things to giver and receiver.

grounding: A student receives help that comes with watching and expectation, and contrasts it with a clean gift that lets the receiver keep dignity.

passage:
Two nights before the project deadline, Keerthana's laptop stopped turning on. She had no money for a repair and the college lab closed at six. Neelam, a senior from the hostel, handed over her own. "Take it. Just return it Sunday."
Keerthana finished the report at 3 am, weak with relief. But on Saturday Neelam texted, "Remember I helped you. Come to my society event tomorrow. Bring your friends." On Sunday, "Why are you always with those girls? I lent you my laptop, you know." Keerthana's stomach tightened each time her phone buzzed.
She returned the laptop that afternoon with a small card: "Thank you. It saved my project. I'll come to the event if I can, but I can't promise more." Neelam stared at the card, then said, "I only wanted to help." Keerthana nodded. "I know. I'd still like to say no when I need to."

qa.q: What happened to Keerthana's laptop two nights before the deadline?
qa.a: It stopped turning on, and she had no money for a repair.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling each time her phone buzzed on Saturday and Sunday?
qa.a: She felt tense and obliged, as her tightening stomach shows. She was grateful for the laptop but uneasy that the help was being kept as a debt.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that separated her thanks from the strings?
qa.a: She returned the laptop with a card thanking Neelam, said she could not promise more, and stated she would like to say no when needed.

qa.q: What might Neelam have been feeling when she stared at the card and said she only wanted to help?
qa.a: Neelam may have felt hurt or surprised, perhaps not realising how her reminders sounded. She might have been hoping for closeness in return.

grounding: A student receives borrowed help and then feels obliged and watched because it carries expectations.

passage:
In my first term, Mehak, a final-year student, lent me her old laptop and a folder of notes. I was so grateful I nearly cried. It felt like the kindest thing anyone had done since I left Nagpur.
By November it felt different. Mehak would ask, loudly in the canteen, "Anjali, did you use my notes for the quiz? What did you get?" She signed me up for her dance society without asking and said, "You'll come, na? After everything." Once she texted to ask why I'd been "offline all evening."
I started walking the long way round the canteen.
Compare that with Rosie aunty in the mess, who slipped me a flask of rasam when I had a cold and never mentioned it again. I still feel warm when I think of it. With Mehak, I mostly feel like I owe rent.

qa.q: What did Mehak lend the narrator in the first term?
qa.a: She lent her old laptop and a folder of notes.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel about Mehak's help by November?
qa.a: Anjali felt obliged and watched, as if owing rent, uncomfortable enough to walk the long way round the canteen.

qa.q: What small step could Anjali try with Mehak?
qa.a: Anjali could thank Mehak once more, offer to return the laptop, and say plainly that the dance society isn't for her.

qa.q: How does Rosie aunty's rasam differ for Anjali?
qa.a: Rosie aunty never mentioned it again, so the gift left Anjali feeling cared for and free rather than in debt.

grounding: Shows a student receiving help that slowly carries hidden expectations, leaving the narrator feeling obliged and watched, compared with a clean gift.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Girls' Hostel B, second week of March.
Pooja (19) came in quiet and kept her dupatta twisted in her hands. In January a senior, Madhuri, gave her a full set of second-hand textbooks and her old cycle. Pooja described it as "the best welcome." Since then, Madhuri has asked her to fetch her tiffin daily, to wait for her after late lectures, and last week told the corridor, "Pooja wouldn't even have books without me." Pooja said, "I can't say no to her. I'll look ungrateful." She has stopped going to the common room.
We talked about the difference between a gift and a loan with conditions. Pooja decided to thank Madhuri, return the cycle, and keep the books. I told the warden to watch for any teasing in the corridor and will see Pooja again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Madhuri tell the corridor last week?
qa.a: She said, 'Pooja wouldn't even have books without me.'

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she said she couldn't say no to Madhuri?
qa.a: Pooja felt trapped and afraid of looking ungrateful, with the gift now weighing on her instead of helping.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: They helped Pooja name the difference between a gift and a conditional loan, supported her plan, alerted the warden and booked a follow-up, so she isn't handling it alone.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see the situation?
qa.a: Madhuri may truly think she was kind and is owed some loyalty, without noticing that the demands make Pooja feel small.

grounding: Shows a student who received gifts slowly feeling obliged and watched as the giver attaches demands, and a counsellor helping her regain dignity.

passage:
Thursday night
Sumit paid for my canteen lunch again today. That's the sixth time. At first it felt sweet. The first day he just said, "My treat, you look tired," and I thought, what a nice boy.
Now he sits next to me every lunch. Today he asked where I was at eleven. I was in the library! Why am I explaining myself? Then he laughed and said, "Arre, relax, you owe me six lunches anyway." Everyone laughed. I didn't.
Tonight Jaya gave me her old jacket because my hostel room is freezing. She just said, "Keep it, it doesn't fit me," and went back to her phone. I'm wearing it now. It feels different. Nothing hangs off it.
Tomorrow I'm going to pay for my own lunch, and his too, and say thank you properly. 😕
Shalini

qa.q: How many times had Sumit paid for Shalini's lunch?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Sumit said she owed him six lunches?
qa.a: Shalini felt uncomfortable and watched, as if the lunches had turned into a debt Sumit could use to check up on Shalini.

qa.q: What would you advise Shalini for tomorrow?
qa.a: The plan to pay and thank Sumit is fine; Shalini could also tell him calmly that being asked where Shalini has been is not okay.

qa.q: How is Jaya's jacket different for Shalini?
qa.a: Jaya gave it and moved on, so Shalini can simply enjoy it with nothing hanging off it.

grounding: Shows a student who slowly feels obliged and watched after repeated treats, contrasted with a gift given with no strings.

passage:
Rafiq: Did you use the lab manual I gave you?
Anjali: Yes, thanks again, it really helped.
Rafiq: Good. Btw saw you at the canteen with Mehul's group, not with us.
Anjali: Just had tea there.
Rafiq: Ok. Just saying, I've done a lot for you this sem.
Anjali: I know. I'm grateful.
Rafiq: So you're coming for the fest committee thing on Sunday na?
Anjali: I have my cousin's engagement on Sunday.
Rafiq: Hmm. After the manual, the notes, the cycle... thought you'd make time.
Anjali typed "sorry", deleted it, typed it again, deleted it again. She looked at the borrowed manual on her shelf. Then she wrote: "I'll return the manual and the cycle tomorrow. Thank you for all of it. I can't come on Sunday."
Rafiq: ?

qa.q: What event does Anjali have on Sunday?
qa.a: She has her cousin's engagement on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she kept typing and deleting "sorry"?
qa.a: She felt torn and guilty, obliged because of all the help, yet uneasy about being watched and pushed.

qa.q: What small step helped Anjali keep her dignity?
qa.a: Returning the manual and the cycle with a clear thank-you and a plain no let her close the debt without apologising for her own plans.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see his own help?
qa.a: He may see it as kindness that earns loyalty in return, without noticing that the hidden expectation makes Anjali feel watched.

grounding: Shows a student who accepted a senior's help beginning to feel obliged and watched because the help came with hidden expectations.
